title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
1. *From Arrian's Epictetus, against the man who held forth on substance.*
What does it matter to me, he says, whether the things that exist are composed of atoms, or of indivisible parts, or of fire and earth? Is it not enough to learn the nature of good and evil, and the limits of desire and aversion, and likewise of impulse and refusal, and, using these as our standards, to manage the affairs of life — leaving alone those questions that are above us, which are perhaps beyond the grasp of the human mind, or which, even if one grants that they are most certainly graspable, are of no use once grasped? And must we not say that those who reckon such matters as necessary to the philosopher's account are making trouble for themselves over nothing? — Is then the precept at Delphi also superfluous, the "Know thyself"? — No, he says, that one is not. — What, then, is its force? If someone gave a dancer in a chorus the order to know himself, would he not heed the command by attending also to his fellow dancers and to keeping in harmony with them? — He would, he says. — And if it were given to a sailor? Or to a soldier? Does it seem to you, then, that man was made to be a creature on his own, or for fellowship? — For fellowship. — By whom? — By Nature. — What that Nature is, and how it governs the whole, and whether it exists or not — is it any longer necessary to busy ourselves with these things?
2. *From Arrian's Epictetus.*
The man who is vexed at what is present and given by fortune is a layman in the conduct of life; but the man who bears these things nobly, and reasons soundly about what comes of them, deserves to be reckoned a good man.
3. *From the same.*
All things obey the universe and serve it: earth and sea and sun and the rest of the stars, and the plants and animals of the earth. Our own body too obeys it, in sickness and in health, growing young and growing old and passing through its other changes, whenever the universe wills. It is reasonable, then, that the one thing which is within our power — that is, our judgment — should not, alone, set itself against it. For the universe is strong and mightier than we, and has taken better counsel for us, in governing us together with the whole. And besides this, opposition, joined to unreason and accomplishing nothing further, only makes us toil in vain and fall into pains and griefs.
4. *From Rufus, out of Epictetus, On Friendship.*
Of all that exists, some things God has placed within our power, and some not within our power. Within our power he placed the finest and most excellent thing, by which indeed he himself is happy — the use of impressions. For this, when it is done rightly, is freedom, an even flow of life, cheerfulness, steadfastness; and this is also justice and law and self-command and the whole of virtue. All the rest he made not to be within our power. We too, therefore, must side with God, and, dividing things in this same way, must lay claim by every means to what is within our power, but entrust what is not within our power to the universe; and whether it asks for our children, or our country, or our body, or anything whatever, gladly give it up.
5. *From Rufus, out of Epictetus, On Friendship.*
Who among us does not admire the deed of Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian? Blinded in one eye by one of his citizens, he received the young man from the people to punish as he himself pleased; yet he refrained from this, and instead educated him and made him a good man, and brought him forward into the theater. When the Lacedaemonians marveled, he said: "This man I received from you insolent and violent; I give him back to you fair-minded and a good citizen."

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
6. *From Rufus, out of Epictetus, On Friendship.*
But beyond all else, it is the work of Nature to bind together and fit our impulse to the impression of what is becoming and useful.
7. *From the same.*
To think that we shall be held in contempt by others unless we injure our worst enemies by every means — that belongs to men utterly base and senseless. For we say that a man is held contemptible insofar as he is unable to do harm; but he is far more truly held contemptible insofar as he is unable to do good.
8. *From Rufus, out of Epictetus, On Friendship.*
Such is the nature of the universe — it was, and is, and shall be — and it is not possible for the things that come to be to come about otherwise than as they now stand. And of this turning and change not only men have a share, and the other animals upon the earth, but the divine things too, and, by Zeus, the four elements themselves turn upward and downward and change: earth becomes water, and water air, and this in turn changes into ether; and the same manner of change runs from above to below. If a man tries to incline his mind toward these things and to persuade himself to accept willingly what is necessary, he will pass through life with great measure and harmony.
10. "Without doing, only as far as speaking."
"Man, where are you throwing it? Look first whether the vessel is clean. For if you pour these things into your conceit, they are lost; if it goes rotten, it has turned to urine, or vinegar, or something worse than these."
More in the Cynic vein: "Bear" and "forbear."
11. *From Arrian's Hortatory Discourses.*
When Archelaus sent for Socrates, meaning to make him rich, Socrates bade them carry back this answer: that "at Athens four quarts of barley meal may be had for an obol, and the springs run with water." For if what I have is not sufficient for me, still I am sufficient for it, and so it too is sufficient for me. Or do you not see that Polus acted the tyrant Oedipus no more sweetly or pleasingly than he did the wanderer and beggar at Colonus? Then shall the man of noble birth show himself worse than Polus, by not playing well every part that the divinity sets upon him? Will he not imitate Odysseus, who in his rags shone no less than in his thick purple cloak?
12. *From Arrian.*
There are some great-souled men who, gently and quietly and as it were without anger, do all the same things as those who are carried away by violent passion. We must guard, then, against the error of such men too, as being far worse than the anger of the man who strains himself in rage. For these last quickly have their fill of vengeance, but the others draw it out long, like men in a slow fever.
13. *From the Memorabilia of Epictetus.*
But I see, says someone, the noble and good perishing of hunger and cold. — And do you not see those who are not noble and good perishing of luxury and bragging and vulgarity? — But it is shameful to be fed at another's expense. — And who, you wretch, feeds himself out of himself, other than the universe? So whoever blames Providence because the wicked go unpunished, because they are strong and rich, acts much as if, when men had lost their eyes, he said they had gone unpunished because their nails were sound. For I say that virtue differs from vice far more than eyes differ from nails.
14. *From the Memorabilia of Epictetus.*
[. . .] bringing forward those austere philosophers who hold that pleasure is not according to nature, but supervenes upon the things that are according to nature — upon justice, self-command, freedom. Why then does the soul rejoice and grow calm over the goods of the body, which are the lesser ones, as Epicurus says, but takes no pleasure in its own goods, which are the greatest? And yet Nature has given me a sense of shame, and I blush deeply whenever I suppose I am saying something shameful. It is this very movement that will not let me set down pleasure as the good and the end of life.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
15. *From the Memorabilia of Epictetus.*
At Rome the women have Plato's Republic in their hands, because he holds that wives should be held in common. For they fix their minds on the words, and not on the man's meaning — that he does not bid one man marry and dwell with one woman and then wishes wives to be held in common, but rather abolishes that kind of marriage and brings in another kind. And, in sum, men delight to furnish excuses for their own faults; whereas philosophy says that it is not fitting to stretch out so much as a finger without good reason.
16. *From the Memorabilia of Epictetus.*
One must know that it is not easy for a settled conviction to take hold in a man, unless day by day he says and hears the same things, and at the same time applies them to his life.
17. *From Epictetus.*
When we have been invited to a banquet, we take what is set before us; and if anyone should bid the host serve him fish or cakes, he would seem out of place. Yet in the universe we ask the gods for things they do not give, and that when there are many things they have already given us.
18. *From the same.*
They are charming, he said, the men who pride themselves on what is not within our power. "I," says one, "am better than you, for I have many estates, while you are pinched with hunger." Another says, "I am of consular rank." Another, "I am a procurator." Another, "I have curly hair." But horse does not say to horse, "I am better than you, for I possess much fodder and plenty of barley, and my bridles are of gold and my saddlecloths embroidered" — rather, "I am swifter than you." And every creature is better or worse by its own virtue or vice. Is man, then, the one creature that has no virtue of its own, so that we must look to hair and clothes and ancestors?
19. The sick are vexed at a physician who gives them no advice, and think they have been given up for lost by him. Why then should a man not be so disposed toward the philosopher, as to suppose he has been given up as past hope of ever becoming sensible, if the philosopher tells him nothing useful?
20. *From the same.*
Those whose bodies are in good condition endure both heat and cold; so too those whose souls are in good condition bear anger and grief and excessive joy and the other passions.
21. *From Epictetus.*
For this reason it is just to praise Agrippinus, that though he was a man of the highest worth he never praised himself, but blushed if anyone else praised him. This man, he said, was of such a kind that he would write a commendation of every hardship that befell him: if he had a fever, of the fever; if he was in disrepute, of disrepute; if he was exiled, of exile. And once, he said, when he was about to lunch, a man came to him with word that Nero ordered him into exile; and he replied: "Well then, we shall lunch at Aricia."
22. Agrippinus, when he was a governor, used to try to persuade those he condemned that it was fitting for them to be condemned. "For it is not as an enemy," he said, "nor as a robber that I cast my vote against them, but as a guardian and protector — just as the physician comforts the man he is cutting and persuades him to submit himself."
23. *From Epictetus.*
Wonderful is Nature, and, as Xenophon says, a lover of life. This body of ours, the most disagreeable and filthiest of all things, we cherish and tend; for if we had to tend our neighbor's body for just five days, we could not endure it. Consider what it is to rise at dawn and brush another man's teeth, and, after he has relieved some need, to wash those parts. Truly it is a wonder to love a thing for which we perform so many services every day. I stuff this sack here, then I empty it; what is more burdensome than this? But I must serve God. For this reason I stay and put up with washing this wretched little body, feeding it, sheltering it. And when I was younger it laid yet another command on me, and even so I bore with it. Why then will you not bear with it, when Nature, who gave us the body, takes it away? — I love it, he says. — But, as I was just saying, was it not Nature who gave you this very loving of it? And the same Nature now says: "Let it go at last, and trouble yourself with it no more."

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
24. *From the same.*
If a man dies young, he blames the gods that he has trouble laid on him when he ought already to have been at rest; and yet, no less, when death draws near, he wants to live, and sends for the physician, and begs him to spare no zeal or care. Wonderful, he said, are men, who neither wish to live nor to die.
25. *From Epictetus.*
Against whoever you set yourself with menace and threat, remember to warn him first that you are a gentle man; and having done nothing savage, you will pass your days without regret and without reproach.
26. You are a little soul carrying a corpse about, as Epictetus used to say.
27. He said one must discover a craft concerning assent, and, in the field that concerns the impulses, keep the faculty of attention — so that they be made with reservation, that they be social, that they be according to merit; and to abstain altogether from desire, and to use aversion toward none of the things not within our power.
28. The contest, he said, is not over some ordinary matter, but over being sane or mad.
28a. Socrates used to say: "What do you want? To have the souls of rational beings, or of irrational ones?" "Of rational beings." "Of what sort of rational beings — sound, or worthless?" "Sound." "Why then do you not seek it?" "Because we have it." "Why then do you fight and quarrel?"
29. *From Epictetus's Manual.*
In everything take thought for nothing so much as for safety; for it is safer to keep silent than to speak. And let go any speaking that will be empty of sense and open to reproach [. . .]
30. There is no fitting out a ship from a single anchor, nor a life from a single hope. *From the same.*
31. *From the same.*
We must stride across, so far as we can, with both our legs and our hopes.
32. It is more needful to heal the soul than the body; for death is better than living badly.
33. *From the same.*
Of pleasant things, those that come most rarely give the most delight. *From the same.*
34. *From the same.*
If a man should overstep the measure, the most delightful things would become the least delightful.
35. No one is free who is not master of himself.
36. Truth is a thing immortal and everlasting; it furnishes us not with a beauty that withers with time, nor with a freedom of speech that justice takes away, but with the just and the lawful, distinguishing from them the unjust, and bringing it to conviction.
1. *Of Epictetus.* Honor the gods with a just and measured disposition, and do not flatter them with extravagant offerings; for the god takes no joy in flattery, nor does the flatterer honor the divine.
Sacrifice to the gods not when you have grown rich, but when you have grown wise; for to be rich belongs even to the ill-fortuned, but to be wise belongs to the happy alone.
2. Do not ask of the gods unbroken health of body, but rather receive continually self-command of soul; and then you will neither fall sick easily, nor, when sick, be ill content.
3. Do not ask of the gods the things you desire, but ask of them rather to be rid of the desire itself. The gods hearken to you then, when you pray not for what is pleasant but for what is good; and they give you good things then, when you take joy not in pleasure but in virtue.
4. Remember to ask great things of the great; for they would not grant petty ones. Nothing is greater or higher than god. When you pray, then, to the gods, ask for divine things, things that no fleshly and earthbound passion touches.
5. As you do not hate the bee for its sting, but tend it for its fruit, so do not turn away from a friend for his rebuke, but love him for his goodwill.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
6. Flatterers are like drones: idle, stingless, and devouring the toils of others. The envious are like wasps: stinging, helpless, ungiving, and useless. But honest men are like bees: hardworking, self-reliant, good managers of their household, plentiful, gentle, ready to rebuke, and sociable. So, if you wish, being a friend, to pass your life among many friends, imitate the bee: let your hive be kept clean of drones and wasps.
7. Test those who present themselves to you for friendship, not by what they give to you, but by what they have won, and granted, and pledged, and bestowed upon themselves.
8. It is not money that makes a friend, but the friend who is money. Money could never produce friendship, any more than earth could produce a god; but friendship could acquire money too in other ways, just as a god could acquire earth.
1. A life entangled with fortune is like a torrent stream: turbulent, full of mud, hard to ford, tyrannical, loud, and short-lived.
2. A soul that keeps company with virtue is like an ever-flowing spring: clean, untroubled, sweet to drink, wholesome, sociable, abundant, harmless, and undying.
3. If you wish to be good, first believe that you are bad.
4. It is better to err seldom while owning that you act amiss, than to act amiss often while claiming you rarely fail.
5. Chastise the passions, so that you may not be punished by them.
6. Do not so much be ashamed of the disgrace that comes from reputation as flee the disgrace that comes from truth.
7. If you wish to be well spoken of, learn to speak well; and having learned to speak well, try to act well, and so you will reap the reward of being well spoken of.
8. Examine yourself, whether you wish to be rich or to be happy. If to be rich, know that this is neither a good nor wholly within your power; if to be happy, know that this is both a good and within your power. For the one is a passing loan of fortune, while happiness is the work of moral choice.
9. As, when you behold a viper or an asp or a scorpion in a casket of ivory or gold, you do not love it or call it blessed for the costliness of the material, but, because its nature is destructive, you turn from it and loathe it — so too, when you see vice lodged in wealth and the pomp of fortune, do not be dazzled by the brilliance of the material, but despise the baseness in the character.
10. Wealth is not among the goods, extravagance is among the evils, self-command is among the goods. Self-command summons us to frugality and to the acquisition of goods, but wealth summons us to extravagance and draws us away from self-command. It is hard, then, for a rich man to be temperate, or a temperate man to be rich.
11. As, if you had been sown or born aboard a ship, you would not be eager to become its helmsman [. . .] for there the ship will not by nature be yours, nor here will wealth, but in every case reason will be. So whatever is natural and akin to you, namely reason, deem this your own and take care of it.
12. Had you been born among the Persians, you would not be eager to dwell in Greece, but to fare well staying where you were. Born then into poverty, why are you eager to grow rich, instead of faring well staying where you are?
13. As it is better to be healthy on a small cot than to lie sick on a broad couch, so it is better to be of good cheer, drawn in within a small competence, than to be downcast amid a great one.
14. It is not poverty that breeds grief, but desire; nor does wealth free a man from fear, but reasoning. If, then, you acquire reasoning, you will neither desire wealth nor complain of poverty.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
15. Neither does a horse pride itself and grow vain over its manger and trappings and rugs, nor a bird over its food and nest, but both over their swiftness — the one of foot, the other of wing. So you too should not give yourself great airs over food and shelter and, in a word, your outward abundance, but over kindness and well-doing.
16. To live well differs from living extravagantly. The one arises from self-command and self-sufficiency and good order and decency and frugality; the other from licentiousness and luxury and disorder and unseemliness. The end of the one is true praise, of the other blame. If, then, you wish to live well, do not seek to be praised for extravagance.
17. Let the first satisfying of your appetite be your measure for all food and drink; let the relish and the pleasure be the appetite itself. Then you will neither take more than you need, nor stand in want of cooks, and you will be content with whatever drink comes your way.
18. Make your meals not extravagant and gloomy, but bright and frugal, so that souls may not be troubled on account of the body, nor, beguiled by bodily pleasures, hold the body in contempt — bodies that take harm by indulging now and falling sick hereafter.
19. Take care that it is not the food in your belly that lifts you up, but the good cheer in your soul; for the former is cast off as refuse and flows away [along with the praise], while the latter, even when the soul departs, remains forever undefiled.
20. At feasts remember that you are entertaining two guests, body and soul; and whatever you give to the body you have at once poured away, but whatever you give to the soul you keep forever.
21. Do not bring anger mingled together with extravagance. Extravagance, leaping upon the body, soon takes its leave; but anger, sinking into the soul, remains for the longest time. Take care, then, lest, carried away by anger, you outrage your guests extravagantly, but rather with gentleness give them frugal cheer.
22. It is shameful, while sweetening one's swallow with the bees' gifts, to embitter with vice that gift of the gods, our reason.
23. At your meals let it be your care that those who serve you not outnumber those they serve; for it is out of place that many souls should be slaves to a few couches.
24. Best of all is it if, working with your own hands in the preparations and feasting at the table, you share the food at hand with those who attend you. But if such a thing is awkward to the occasion, remember that you, not weary, are served by the weary; that you eat, served by those not eating; that you drink, served by those not drinking; that you talk, served by those keeping silent; that you are at ease, served by those held in check. So you will neither, growing inflamed yourself, suffer something out of place, nor, provoking another, work him a grievous wrong.
25. To wrangle and contend is everywhere unbecoming, but most unseemly in the talk over wine. For neither could a drunken man teach a sober one, nor again could a drunken man be persuaded by a sober one. And where there is no end of persuasion at hand, you offer yourself up to strain in vain.
26. The cicadas are musical, but the snails are mute; the one delights in being made wet, the other in being warmed. Then the dew calls forth the snails, and at it they come out; but the blazing sun rouses the cicadas, and at it they sing. So, if you wish to be a musical and well-tuned man, then, when at the drinking your soul is bedewed with wine, do not let it go forth to be defiled; but when in the councils it is set ablaze by reason, then bid it utter and sing the oracles of justice.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
27. Consider the man you talk with in one of three ways: as better, or as worse, or as your equal. If better, you must listen to him and be persuaded by him; if worse, persuade him; if equal, agree with him; and so you will never be caught in contentiousness.
28. It is better, yielding to truth, to overcome opinion than, yielding to opinion, to be overcome by truth.
29. Seeking truth, you will not seek to win by every means; and having found truth, you will have the gift of not being overcome.
30. Truth wins by its own resources, but opinion by what lies outside.
31. Freedom and slavery — the one is the name of virtue, the other of vice, and both are works of moral choice. Of things in which moral choice has no part, neither touches; but fortune is wont to be master of the body and of all things about the body that have no share in moral choice. For no one is a slave whose moral choice is free.
32. An evil bond of the body is fortune, of the soul, vice. For the man freed in body but bound in soul is a slave; while the man bound in body but freed in soul is free.
33. The bond of the body is loosed both by Nature through death and by vice through money; but the bond of the soul is loosed by virtue, through learning and experience and training.
34. If you wish to live untroubled and well content, try to have all who dwell with you good. And you will have them good if you educate the willing, and let the unwilling go once they have been brought into hand. For wickedness will flee away together with those who flee, and slavery with them; but goodness will remain behind with those who stay with you, and freedom too.
35. It is better, living with one free man, to be fearless and free, than, living with many, to be a slave.
36. What you flee from suffering, do not set about inflicting. You flee slavery; guard, then, against enslaving others. For in submitting to enslave others, you seem first to have been a slave yourself; since virtue has no part with vice, nor freedom with slavery.
37. As a healthy man would not wish to be tended by the sick, nor that those who dwell with him be sick, so neither would the free man endure to be served by slaves, or that those who share his life be slaves.
38. If you wish to be without slaves, free yourself first from slavery; and you will be free if you free yourself from desire. For neither Aristides nor Epaminondas nor Lycurgus, by being rich and waited on by slaves, were proclaimed — the one the Just, another the Savior, another a god; rather it was because, living in poverty, they freed Greece from slavery.
39. If you wish your household to be well ordered, imitate the Spartan Lycurgus. For just as he fenced his city not with walls but fortified its inhabitants with virtue, and so kept the city free forever, so you too should not throw up a great courtyard and raise lofty towers, but stay your household with goodwill and faith and friendship; and nothing harmful will enter it, not even if the whole array of vice should marshal against it.
40. Do not encircle your house with panels and paintings, but inscribe it with self-command. For the one is a passing bewitchment of the eyes, but the other an inborn, indelible, and everlasting adornment of a house.
41. Instead of a herd of cattle, try to gather herds of friends to flock about your house.
42. As the wolf resembles the dog, so too the flatterer and the adulterer and the parasite resemble the friend. Take care, then, lest, in place of guard dogs, you unwittingly take in ravening wolves.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
43. To be eager that one's house, whitened with plaster, be admired belongs to a man of vulgar taste; but to make one's character bright by the kindness of fellowship belongs to a man who loves what is fine and loves his fellow men alike.
44. If you admire small things before great ones, you will be despised; but if you greatly despise the small, you will be admired.
45. Nothing is meaner than love of gain, love of pleasure, and boastfulness; nothing is greater than greatness of soul, gentleness, love of mankind, and well-doing.
46. No man who loves money and pleasure and reputation loves his fellow men; only the man who loves what is fine.
47. As you would not wish, sailing in a great and elegant and gold-laden ship, to be sunk, so neither choose, lodging in a vast and costly house, to be storm-tossed.
48. As a true balance is neither set right by a true balance nor judged by a false one, so too the just judge is neither set right by the just nor judged by the unjust.
49. As the straight has no need of the straight, so neither does the just have need of the just.
50. Do not sit in judgment in another's court before you yourself have been judged before Justice.
51. If you wish to render judgments justly, take no note of any of the litigants who plead their cause, but only of Justice herself.
52. You will stumble least in your judgments if you yourself go through life without stumbling.
53. It is better, having judged justly, to be unjustly blamed by the man condemned, than, having judged unjustly, to be justly reproached before Nature.
54. As the touchstone that tests gold is not in turn itself tested by the gold, so too is the man who holds the standard of judgment.
55. It is shameful for the judge to be judged by others.
56. As nothing is straighter than the straight, so nothing is juster than the just.
57. As the beacons on the harbors, kindling a great flame from a few faggots, render sufficient aid to the ships wandering over the sea, so too a brilliant man in a storm-tossed city, content himself with little, confers great benefits on his fellow citizens.
58. As, if you set about steering a ship, you would by all means learn thoroughly the helmsman's craft [. . .] for it will be open to you, just as there to steer every ship, so here too to steer every city.
59. If it lies before you to adorn the city with offerings, dedicate first to yourself the fairest offering of gentleness and justice and well-doing.
60. You will benefit the city most greatly if you raise not the roofs but the souls. For it is better that great souls dwell in small houses than that mean slaves lurk in great ones.
61. Do not deck the walls of your dwelling with stones from Euboea and Sparta, but rather adorn the breasts of the citizens and of those who govern with the schooling that comes from Greece. For cities are well ordered by the counsels of men, and not by stones and timbers.
62. As, if you wished to rear lions, you would not concern yourself with the costliness of their cages but with the conduct of the beasts, so, if you undertake to lead the citizens, do not trouble yourself so much over the costliness of buildings as take care for the courage of those who dwell in them.
63. As a good colt-breaker does not feed the good colts but let the unruly ones starve, but feeds both alike and chastises the one the more, forcing it to come level with the other, so too a caring man, skilled in the art of statesmanship, undertakes to make some of the citizens fair-minded; the rest, on the other hand, he does not let go utterly to ruin, but grudges neither of them their nurture, and educates and spurs on more sharply the one who sets himself against reason and law.

title: Fragments and Gnomologium
text:
64. As neither is a goose dismayed by a cackle nor a sheep by a bleat, so let not the voice of a senseless crowd dismay you.
65. As a crowd asking you indiscriminately for something of your own does not abash you, so neither let a mob, unjustly putting you to shame, throw you into confusion.
66. Whatever falls to your lot to contribute to the city, contribute it before you are asked; and you will never be asked for what does not fall to you.
67. As the sun does not wait for prayers and enchantments in order to rise, but straightway shines and is greeted by all, so neither should you wait for applause and noise and praises in order to do good, but do good willingly, and you will be loved on equal terms with the sun.
